title: Charging QBC for OBR projects.
problem_description:
The lesson learned pertains to the consumption of traffic in the roaming project.

We are utilizing the converged core, which ensures that all traffic consumption is reported to the CHF. However, it is important to note that we are not reconciling the traffic using CDRs or any other method to report it to the visitor network.

To address this, we are employing QBC (QoS Flow-Based Charging), which differs from FBC (Flow-Based Charging). QBC reports all traffic based on QoS flows rather than RG (Rating Groups) or service IDs associated with the type of traffic generated by the UE. This distinction is crucial because RGs and SIDs configured for visitor and home networks may not align with the equipment configurations.

Additionally, in the case of video calls, QBC reports two QoS flows: one for the signaling component and another for the video traffic. When comparing traffic reported by FBC and QBC, the total traffic should remain consistent.

Another critical aspect is the configuration of QBC. To enable QBC charging functionality, it is necessary to activate this feature within the SMF charging profile. Furthermore, if local triggers are required, you must configure or create an event-trigger-QBC within the charging profile.

BR,
technical_solution: To test with the customer and compare the traffic reported by FBC, we configured the QBC (QoS Flow-Based Charging) triggers and enabled the QBC functionality within the SMF charging profile

title: CMM26.7 SW Release the security hardening disabled the legacy scp
problem_description: According to L4, the SCP command used for transferring files was disabled for security reasons in CMM26.7 SW Release.
technical_solution:
Use SFTP instead of legacy SCP, SFTP is preferred over SCP due to its enhanced security, robust protocol, and richer feature set, offering an interactive and more reliable file transfer experience.

We can use a single sftp command to directly download a file from a remote server to your local home folder.

sftp username@remote_host:/path/to/remote/file ~/

title: Alarms are not in sync between CMM 26.7.0.1 and NetAct. NetAct shows alarrms that are not active in CMM
problem_description: At the NetAct level, alarms are still being received that appear as cancelled in the CMM. We cannot delete them in the MME because they are not active, and it is impossible to delete historical information. We already tried refreshing the processes by switching the NEC, but the problem persists. NetAct support states that if they appear there, it is because they are real, but what we observe on the CMM side is that they should not be present. CMM is running 26.7.0.1
technical_solution:
Maintenance mode removed on netact and applied the procedure suggested on this case 05870255

After the restart, the historical/stale alarm entry is no longer returned by SNMP.

Regarding the workaround procedure we always recommend executing it during a MW, no impact is expected.

Workaround: Restart the snmpagent process on the ALMS pod:

# 1. Take a backup for the entire /var/log folder in alms0.

# 2. Login to alms0 as a root user.
-su appuser
-ssh alms0
-su root
Check the alarm
# 3. Check current snmpservice status, PID will be different. NOTE: If STAT is other than "Sl", stop the procedure.
supervisorctl status snmpagent
  # Expected output:
  # snmpagent RUNNING pid 3674453, uptime 0:02:23
ps -o pid,stat,cmd -p $(pgrep -f '/nokia/snmpagent/snmpservice.py')
  # Expected output:
  # PID STAT CMD
  # 3674453 Sl python3 /opt/nokia/lib64/python3.9/site-packages/nokia/snmpagent/snmpservice.py

# 4. Restart snmpservice. STAT in "R" is expected.
supervisorctl stop snmpagent
supervisorctl start snmpagent
ps -o pid,stat,cmd -p $(pgrep -f '/nokia/snmpagent/snmpservice.py')
  # Expected output:
  # PID STAT CMD
  # 3674453 R python3 /opt/nokia/lib64/python3.9/site-packages/nokia/snmpagent/snmpservice.py

# 5. Wait ~2 minutes, and check snmpservice status.
ps -o pid,stat,cmd -p $(pgrep -f '/nokia/snmpagent/snmpservice.py')
  # Expected output:
  # PID STAT CMD
  # 3674453 Sl python3 /opt/nokia/lib64/python3.9/site-packages/nokia/snmpagent/snmpservice.py

# 6. Check again the alarm

after this the alarms disappeared

title: userLocationInformation Feild Missing in 5GCDR
problem_description:
As part of the 5G testing activities, we have observed that the PGW is not including the UserLocationInformation (ULI) in the generated CDRs.

Initially, we added the configuration parameter “include-3gpp-user-location-info-5g” on the PGW. After applying this configuration, we could see that the PGW is sending the ULI information over the Gy interface; however, the same information is still not being included in the CDRs.
technical_solution:
The parameter “nr-user-location-info” is to include location5G record extension field in CDRs which is received from the AMF. It won’t have any service impact, it will just add the 5G ULI in CDRs

The following conditions apply:
• This field is present only when the SMF Legacy Charging is enabled.
• 5G ULI is transparently copied to the location5G field. The location5G field is not present in every CDR of the session; only when 5G ULI attribute is received.
• Changes of the 5G location do not trigger the closure of a location5G container. You can control, with the use-last-known-uli command, if the 5G ULI value is valid when the container is open or closed.

title: Trace capture procedure on VSR of a VNF based CMM with M IPDS architecture
problem_description:
Hi,
VSR is the first touch point of a VNF based CMM (with M IPDS architecture) for leaf/spine switches. So, sometimes it becomes essential to capture pcap on VSR to identify and troubleshoot IP connectivity or application-level issues. VSR use SROS instead of linux based OS. So, the trace capture method is different from that of IPDS or other linux based VMs.
The pcap trace capture for a VSR is mentioned in the below section. This facility is available in all release of VNF based CMM.
technical_solution:
Before we start:
There are 4 ports in a VSR in a VNF based CMM:
Port 1/1/1 is for uplink
Port 1/1/2 is for cross connect between VSR
Port 1/1/3 is single homing towards IPDS
Port 1/1/4 is multi homing towards IPDS

Adjust the ports in the below MOP based on specific case requirement. Usually, it is sufficient to capture pcap on port 1/1/1.

VSR trace procedure:
login to the VSR where we want to capture the pcap.
Step 1:
Delete mirror22.pcap file:
file delete mirror22.pcap.

Step 2:
create mirror22.pcap file
file vi mirror22.pcap
without editing press :wq

Step3:
run below config in VSR:

config
echo "Mirror Configuration"
#--------------------------------------------------
    mirror
        mirror-dest 30 name "30" create
            pcap "testpcap" create
                file-url "ftp://127.1.0.2/cf3:/mirror22.pcap"
            exit
            no shutdown
        exit
        mirror-source "30"
            port 1/1/1 egress ingress
port 1/1/2 egress ingress
port 1/1/3 egress ingress
port 1/1/4 egress ingress
            no shutdown
        exit
    exit

exit all

Step 4:
Save the config:
admin save

Step 5:
- to start pcap trace on VSR

debug pcap "testpcap" capture start

Step 6:
- to stop pcap trace on VSR

debug pcap "testpcap" capture stop

Step 7:
check the mirror22.pcap file using below command:
file dir

Step 8:
Download the mirror22.pcap file on necc-0 by doing sftp to the VSR.

Note:
Always make sure to stop trace once the scenario is complete.

title: CMM AMF Registration failure with NRF FQDN Endpoint Configuration
problem_description:
In our deployment, we intend to use the NRF’s FQDN and port 8080, so we configured both the FQDN and the nfIpEndPointListName (with IP set to 0.0.0.0 and port 8080) at the NF service instance level.

According to the documentation, configuring the FQDN and nfIpEndPointListName at the NF service instance level should take precedence over the networkFunctionInstance level. However, we’ve observed that if the FQDN is not also configured at the networkFunctionInstance level, the AMF does not establish the Nnrf link. The documentation does not state that the FQDN must be set at the networkFunctionInstance for NRF selection.
technical_solution:
R&D reviewed the implementation and confirmed that a software correction is required, rather than documentation being wrong/missleading.
The issue is tracked under IMR170294 and is planned to be available in CMM25.7.0.13 ( schedule permitting ), otherwise in CMM25.7.0.14.
The investigation confirmed that the observed behavior is caused by the current CMM implementation.
When the NRF FQDN is provisioned only at the NF Service Instance level, the NRF registration sequence is not initiated.
After the same FQDN is additionally configured at the networkFunctionInstance level, the NRF registration proceeds successfully and the Nnrf link is established.

title: Lesson Learned – Deployment Issues Encountered During CMM Deployment and Resolutions
problem_description: During the CMM deployment, multiple deployment and Kubernetes configuration issues were encountered that impacted pod creation, resource allocation, and network interface initialization. The issues were analyzed and resolved in coordination with the NCP, Cloud, and Fabric teams.
technical_solution:
The following lessons learned and corrective actions were identified:

1. IPDS Pod Memory Limit Exceeded
Issue:
The IPDS pod memory limit exceeded the supported/configured range.

Error:
IPDS pod memory limit exceeded. It should be between 8Gi and 62Gi.

Root Cause:
The IPDS pod memory limit was configured to 71Gi, which was above the maximum supported limit of 62Gi.

Resolution:
The IPDS pod memory limit was reduced from 71Gi to 62Gi, which brought the configuration within the supported range and allowed the deployment to proceed.

Lesson Learned / Preventive Action:

Validate pod resource limits against the supported range before deployment.
Include IPDS pod CPU/memory validation as part of the pre-deployment checklist.
Avoid configuring resource limits beyond the platform-supported maximum.
2. Resource Quota Exceeded – Critical
Issue:
Pod creation was blocked because the Kubernetes resource quota was already fully utilized.

Error:

exceeded quota: tbcmm-resourcequota,
requested: limits.cpu=440,
used: limits.cpu=114,
limited: limits.cpu=114

Root Cause:
The namespace resource quota was insufficient for the requested deployment resources. The configured CPU quota was already fully consumed, preventing the required pods from being created.

Resolution:
The issue was discussed and reviewed with the NCP and Cloud teams. The CPU and memory resource quotas were increased according to the deployment requirements.

Lesson Learned / Preventive Action:

Review namespace CPU and memory quotas before starting deployment.
Compare the expected deployment resource requirements against the available quota.
Ensure sufficient resource quota is provisioned in advance to avoid pod creation failures.
Add resource quota validation to the deployment readiness checklist.
3. Missing Kubernetes Priority Classes – Blocking Pod Creation
Issue:
Required Kubernetes PriorityClasses were missing, which prevented the affected pods from being created/scheduled correctly.

Error:

no PriorityClass with name cmm-non-necc-priority was found
no PriorityClass with name cmm-necc-priority was found

Root Cause:
The required PriorityClass resources were not available in the Kubernetes environment before the CMM deployment was initiated.

Resolution:
The required PriorityClass configurations were identified and configured as follows:

priorityClass: cmm-non-necc-priority
priorityClass: cmm-necc-priority

After configuring the required PriorityClasses, the deployment was able to proceed.

Lesson Learned / Preventive Action:

Verify the existence of all required Kubernetes PriorityClasses before deployment.
Include PriorityClass validation in the pre-deployment checks.
Ensure all cluster-level dependencies are provisioned before application deployment.
4. Multus CNI – Secondary IP Allocation Failure for IPDS Interface
Issue:
The IPDS pod remained in a Pending state because Multus CNI was unable to allocate a secondary IP address for the IPDS interface (eth2).

Error:

Could not allocate IP in range:
IP: 10.118.0.100 / - 10.118.0.101 /
Range: 10.118.0.96/27

Root Cause:
The required secondary IP addresses were not available for allocation from the configured CIQ IP pool/range, resulting in Multus CNI being unable to configure the IPDS secondary interface.

Resolution:
The IP assignments for all dual-IPDS interfaces were reviewed and updated. New IP addresses were allocated from the second-last four available IP addresses in the CIQ IP pool. After updating the IP assignments, the Multus CNI IP allocation issue was resolved and the affected pods were able to proceed.

Lesson Learned / Preventive Action:

Verify IP pool availability before deployment.
Ensure sufficient free IP addresses are reserved for all dual-IPDS interfaces.
Validate the CIQ IP pool against the expected deployment requirements.
Maintain proper IP allocation tracking to avoid conflicts or exhaustion.
Include Multus/IP pool validation as part of the deployment pre-check.

title: IP Pool Distribution Not Working – Troubleshooting and Resolution
problem_description:
Issue Description

IP pools were not being equally distributed. During the investigation, it was observed that IP pool utilization was not balanced, and some pools were not receiving user traffic as expected.
technical_solution:
Initial Investigation
During the investigation, it was found that the following CLI was missing under the Network Realm:
ip-pool-distribution
This CLI is required to enable IP pool distribution and distribute users/traffic across the configured IP pools.
After adding ip-pool-distribution under the Network Realm, the IP pools were still not equally distributed.
Further investigation identified that the following CLI also needs to be configured under the respective IP pool:
use-prefixes-immediately
________________________________________
3. Root Cause
The use-prefixes-immediately CLI need to configure under the IP pool configuration.
However, simply adding this CLI to an already configured IP pool may not take effect immediately.
To make the configuration effective, the affected IP pool needs to be removed from the IP Pool Name configuration and then added again after configuring use-prefixes-immediately.
________________________________________
4. Resolution Procedure
Step 1: Verify IP Pool Distribution
First, verify that the following CLI is configured under the Network Realm:
ip-pool-distribution
If it is missing, add it under the Network Realm.
This configuration is required to distribute traffic/users across the available IP pools.
________________________________________
Step 2: Identify the IP Pool with Zero Traffic Utilization
Before making any configuration changes, check the traffic utilization of all configured IP pools.
Identify the IP pool where the traffic utilization is zero.
Important: Do not remove all IP pools unnecessarily. Remove only the IP pool that has zero traffic utilization and requires the use-prefixes-immediately configuration.
This approach minimizes the impact on active users and avoids unnecessary changes to pools that are already carrying traffic.
________________________________________
Step 3: Remove the Zero-Utilization IP Pool
Remove only the identified zero-utilization IP pool from the IP Pool Name configuration under the Network Realm.
Important: Make sure the selected pool has zero traffic utilization before removing it.
________________________________________
Step 4: Configure use-prefixes-immediately
Under the affected IP pool configuration, add:
use-prefixes-immediately
This configuration is required for the prefix/IP pool to be used immediately after it is configured.
________________________________________
Step 5: Add the IP Pool Again
After adding:
use-prefixes-immediately
add the same IP pool back under the IP Pool Name configuration in the Network Realm.
This reconfiguration is required for the new CLI to take effect.
________________________________________
Step 6: Verify the Distribution
After the configuration takes effect, monitor the IP pool utilization.
Verify that:
• Users are being allocated from the newly configured pool.
• Traffic is being distributed across the available IP pools.
• The previously unused pool starts receiving users/traffic.
• IP pool utilization becomes more balanced.

________________________________________
5. Expected Result
After completing the above procedure, the IP pool should become available for immediate use and new users should be distributed across the configured IP pools.
The previously unused/zero-utilization pool should start receiving user traffic, resulting in better and more balanced IP pool utilization.

title: Enabling includeMappedGummei without RC Change or CMM lock/unlock can cause Subscriber Imbalance in CMM pool
problem_description:
Enabling includeMappedGummei and forcing CMM to send ENB configuration update via RC change or CMM lock/unlock on only one CMM in a pool of three results in asymmetric MME selection behavior during inter-RAT mobility (2G/3G to 4G). The CMM with the parameter enabled will advertise mapped GUMMEIs to eNBs, allowing UEs previously served by its collocated SGSN to be routed back to it. However, the other two CMMs will only advertise their native LTE GUMMEIs. Consequently, UEs moving from 2G/3G areas served by the other two CMMs will not be routed to their original CMMs but will instead be distributed among all three CMMs (or based on eNB load balancing) because the eNBs cannot match the mapped GUMMEI to a specific CMM. This leads to subscriber imbalance and increased inter-CMM signaling (SGSN context requests) for the two CMMs without the feature enabled.

The includeMappedGummei global parameter controls whether the MME includes the SGSN's mapped served GUMMEIs in the S1 Setup Response and MME Configuration Update messages. This feature is critical for maintaining the same physical CMM node during inter-RAT mobility (2G/3G to 4G) in a combined MME/SGSN deployment.

1.	Behavior of the CMM with includeMappedGummei Enabled

*	GUMMEI Advertisement: This CMM advertises both its native LTE GUMMEI and the mapped GUMMEIs derived from its collocated SGSN's configuration (PLMN, LAC, NRI).
*	MME Selection: When a UE moves from a 2G/3G area served by this CMM's SGSN to 4G, the UE maps its P-TMSI to a GUMMEI. The eNB recognizes this mapped GUMMEI in the list provided by this specific CMM and routes the attach/TAU request to this CMM.
*	Result: The UE stays on the same CMM, avoiding inter-CMM mobility and SGSN context requests.

1.	Behavior of the Two CMMs with includeMappedGummei Disabled

*	GUMMEI Advertisement: These CMMs advertise only their native LTE GUMMEIs. They do not advertise the mapped GUMMEIs corresponding to their collocated SGSNs.
*	MME Selection: When a UE moves from a 2G/3G area served by one of these CMMs' SGSNs to 4G, the UE maps its P-TMSI to a GUMMEI. The eNB looks for this mapped GUMMEI in the lists provided by all three CMMs.

*	It will not find a match in the list of the CMM that served the UE in 2G/3G (because that CMM did not advertise the mapped GUMMEI).

*	It may find a match in the list of the third CMM (if the mapped GUMMEI happens to match its advertised mapped GUMMEIs, which is unlikely unless LAC/NRI overlap, but typically it won't).

*	More commonly, the eNB will not find a specific match for the mapped GUMMEI and will fall back to load balancing or round-robin selection among the available CMMs in the pool.

*	Result: The UE is likely to be routed to a different CMM than the one that served it in 2G/3G. This triggers an inter-CMM SGSN context request to retrieve the UE's context from the original CMM's SGSN.

1.	Impact on the Pool

*	Subscriber Imbalance: The CMM with the feature enabled will retain its 2G/3G-to-4G mobile subscribers. The other two CMMs will lose these subscribers to the pool's load balancing mechanism, potentially leading to an uneven distribution of 4G subscribers (SAU) across the three CMMs.
*	Increased Signaling: The two CMMs without the feature enabled will experience increased SGSN context request/response signaling on the Gn interface as they retrieve contexts for UEs that were previously served by their own SGSNs but are now attached to a different CMM.
*	Inconsistent Mobility: The network will exhibit inconsistent inter-RAT mobility behavior. UEs served by the "enabled" CMM in 2G/3G will stay on it in 4G, while UEs served by the "disabled" CMMs in 2G/3G will be randomly distributed among the three CMMs in 4G.

1.	Recommendation For consistent behavior and optimal load balancing in a pool of combined MME/SGSN CMMs, the includeMappedGummei parameter should be enabled on all CMMs and RC change or CMM lock/unlock should be done to force CMM to send mapped GUMMEI in ENB configuration update to all ENBS in the pool. This ensures that all CMMs can retain their respective 2G/3G subscribers during inter-RAT mobility, minimizing inter-CMM signaling and maintaining subscriber balance.
technical_solution: For consistent behavior and optimal load balancing in a pool of combined MME/SGSN CMMs, the includeMappedGummei parameter should be enabled on all CMMs and RC change or CMM lock/unlock should be done to force CMM to send mapped GUMMEI in ENB configuration update to all ENBS in the pool. This ensures that all CMMs can retain their respective 2G/3G subscribers during inter-RAT mobility, minimizing inter-CMM signaling and maintaining subscriber balance.

title: Trusted WLAN IPv4 Parameters (IP4CP)
problem_description:
Hi Expert,

We're testing Trusted Wi-Fi access over the S2a interface between Cisco TWAG and Nokia CMG (CUPS). The UE bearer is created successfully, but immediately after receiving the Create Session Response, the TWAG sends a Delete Session Request.

Cisco indicated that the Trusted WLAN IPv4 Parameters / IPv4 Configuration Parameters (IP4CP) IE is missing from the Create Session Response. We checked the CMG Configuration Guide and found that this IE is not supported.

Do you have any idea how we can handle this case?

Thank you!
